title: The Murle People and Their Language
subtitle: The language, identity, historical relationships and cultural knowledge that connect Murle communities across Boma, Pibor and beyond.
author: Murle Connect Editorial Team

body.heading: ZOOZ O MURLO
paragraphs: Language is one of the strongest foundations of a people's identity. Through language, people name their families, places, animals, plants, ceremonies, relationships and experiences. They tell stories about the past and teach younger generations how their community understands the world.

For the Murle people, the Murle language is an essential part of this cultural inheritance. It connects communities living in the Pibor lowlands, the Boma highlands and other areas where Murle people have settled.

The history of the Murle language is also connected to the wider history of eastern Africa. Murle belongs to the Surmic group of languages, and its closest linguistic relationships provide important evidence about historical connections between communities in the region.

Understanding the Murle language therefore means understanding more than vocabulary and grammar. It means understanding one of the main ways Murle history, identity and cultural knowledge have been carried from one generation to another.

body.heading: What Is the Murle Language?
paragraphs: Murle is the language traditionally spoken by the Murle people. It is spoken principally in eastern South Sudan, especially in the wider Pibor and Boma areas, with Murle-speaking communities also connected to neighbouring regions across the border in southwestern Ethiopia.

The language has its own vocabulary, grammar, sounds and ways of expressing relationships and ideas. Like every living language, Murle has developed over generations and continues to change as its speakers interact with other communities and with the modern world.
Murle is not simply a different accent or dialect of a neighbouring language. It is a distinct language with its own linguistic history and structure.
The continued use of Murle is therefore an important part of maintaining the cultural identity of the people.

body.heading: Murle and the Surmic Language Family
paragraphs: Linguists classify Murle within the Surmic group of languages. Surmic languages are spoken mainly across southwestern Ethiopia and adjoining areas of eastern South Sudan.

The Surmic group includes Murle and several other languages whose speakers have historical and linguistic connections. Among the languages commonly discussed in relation to Murle are Didinga, Tennet and related languages of the wider Surmic area.

Language classification is based on systematic comparison of vocabulary, grammar, sound patterns and other linguistic features. It does not mean that all communities speaking related languages are one modern ethnic group.

The relationship between Murle and other Surmic languages is therefore useful for reconstructing parts of the region's deeper history while recognizing the distinct identities of the peoples who speak those languages today.

body.heading: Language and the History of the Murle
paragraphs: Language provides historians with evidence that can help investigate relationships between populations. When languages share particular words, grammatical structures or sound correspondences, linguists can sometimes reconstruct earlier relationships between their speakers.

For the Murle, linguistic relationships with other Surmic languages support the view that the peoples of this region have a much older history of interaction and connection than modern political borders suggest.

Language does not, however, provide a precise record of every migration. It cannot by itself establish the exact route taken by every Murle ancestor or give a precise date for when a particular community separated from another.
The strongest historical understanding comes when linguistic evidence is considered together with oral traditions, anthropology, historical records and archaeological research.

body.heading: The Murle Language and Oral History
paragraphs: For generations, Murle history was transmitted mainly through speech rather than through written books. Elders played an important role in remembering and communicating knowledge about ancestors, families, places, important events and community traditions.
Stories and accounts of the past could be passed from parents and elders to children through ordinary conversation, ceremonies, songs and other forms of cultural teaching.
This oral tradition helped preserve knowledge even when people were living in different settlements or moving seasonally with livestock.
The Murle language was therefore not simply a means of communication. It was the vehicle through which historical memory travelled from one generation to another.

body.heading: Names and Historical Memory
paragraphs: Place names are particularly important to understanding the relationship between language and history. Names for rivers, hills, settlements, grazing areas and other locations can preserve memories about how people understand their landscape.
When an elder explains the meaning of a place name, the explanation can contain information about an event, a person, an environmental feature or an important period in community history.
Personal names and family names can also carry historical meaning. They can connect people to parents, grandparents, ancestors, events or cultural circumstances.
For this reason, documenting Murle vocabulary and place names is also a way of documenting history.

body.heading: Murle Across Boma and Pibor
paragraphs: Murle is spoken across communities living in different environments. The Boma highlands and Pibor lowlands have different ecological conditions and have encouraged different patterns of livelihood and settlement.
Despite these differences, the Murle language provides an important connection between communities. Speakers can recognize a common linguistic heritage even when local speech may differ.
Differences in pronunciation, vocabulary or expressions can develop naturally when communities live apart or interact with different neighbouring populations.

Such differences should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that the communities are separate peoples. Languages commonly contain regional and social variations while remaining part of the same wider language.

body.heading: Language Change
paragraphs: No living language remains completely unchanged. Languages develop as speakers create new expressions, borrow words, change pronunciation and adapt existing vocabulary to new circumstances.
Murle speakers have interacted with neighbouring communities for generations. Such contact can introduce new words and expressions while the basic identity of the language remains intact.
Modern education, Christianity, government administration, technology, radio, mobile phones, social media and migration have created additional opportunities for language contact.

These changes are normal parts of language development. The important question for cultural preservation is not whether Murle will ever change, but whether future generations will continue to speak, understand, document and value it.

body.heading: Murle and Neighbouring Languages
paragraphs: Murle communities have lived alongside speakers of many other languages. Depending on location and period, contact has occurred with Dinka, Nuer, Toposa, Anyuak, Ethiopian communities and other neighbouring populations.
People who trade, marry, travel, attend school or live near one another often become multilingual. A Murle speaker may therefore know languages other than Murle without losing their Murle identity.
Multilingualism is historically common in regions where different communities interact regularly. It can provide practical advantages while also creating opportunities for cultural exchange.

At the same time, language shift can occur when younger generations increasingly use another language in education, employment or public life. This is one reason why maintaining Murle in homes and communities is important for long-term cultural continuity.

body.heading: Language and Identity
paragraphs: For many communities, language is closely connected to belonging. Speaking Murle can connect a person to family, community history and cultural knowledge.

Language carries concepts that may be difficult to translate perfectly into another language. Words connected to kinship, cattle, age-sets, ceremonies, landscapes and customary relationships can contain meanings shaped by Murle experience.
When a language disappears, more than vocabulary is lost. Traditional ways of describing the world can also disappear.
Protecting Murle language is therefore an important part of protecting Murle cultural identity.

body.heading: Cattle, Land and Language
paragraphs: The importance of cattle in many Murle communities is reflected in the knowledge people need to manage livestock and move through the environment.

A pastoral community requires detailed knowledge of water sources, grazing areas, animal behaviour, seasons and routes. Much of this knowledge is expressed through language and passed between generations.

The same is true of agriculture and the natural environment. Knowledge about crops, soils, rain, rivers, forests, wildlife and medicinal plants can be preserved in specialized vocabulary and oral teaching.
Language therefore provides a record of how Murle communities have understood and interacted with their environment.

body.heading: Language and Social Relationships
paragraphs: Murle society contains detailed systems of social relationships. Family, clan, age-set and community relationships affect how people understand their responsibilities toward one another.
Language provides the terms through which these relationships are identified and communicated. Kinship vocabulary, forms of address and expressions of respect help organize social life.
The words used for relatives and social roles can also preserve distinctions that are important within Murle culture.
Studying this vocabulary can therefore help researchers understand how Murle society has organized relationships across generations.

body.heading: Language and Traditional Knowledge
paragraphs: Traditional knowledge is often stored in language. A community's understanding of weather, livestock, plants, farming, hunting, medicine, ceremonies and social responsibilities can be transmitted orally.
Proverbs are another important example. A proverb can communicate advice or social values in a short expression that carries meaning developed over generations.
Stories can preserve historical memory while songs can communicate emotions, events, praise, criticism and cultural values.
When these forms of knowledge are recorded in Murle, the original language matters because translation can sometimes remove cultural meanings that are difficult to express in another language.

body.heading: The Murle Language in the Modern World
paragraphs: The modern world has created both challenges and opportunities for Murle language preservation.

Children and young people increasingly encounter languages used in schools, government, churches, business, media and digital communication. These languages can become dominant in areas of public life while Murle remains strongest within families and communities.

At the same time, digital technology creates new possibilities. Murle can be recorded in audio and video, written in digital documents, taught through mobile applications and preserved in online archives.
The same technology that accelerates language change can therefore also become a tool for language preservation.

body.heading: Writing Murle
paragraphs: A spoken language does not need a written tradition to be a complete language. Languages around the world have existed for generations through speech and oral transmission.

Writing nevertheless provides an important additional method for preserving language. It allows stories, vocabulary, proverbs, historical accounts and educational materials to be recorded and shared across generations.

Writing Murle requires careful attention to its sound system and to the ways speakers themselves use the language. A practical writing system should therefore be developed and refined with the participation of fluent Murle speakers, educators and language researchers.
Digital documentation should also preserve the original spelling and pronunciation choices used by the community rather than imposing unnecessary changes from another language.

body.heading: The Importance of Elders
paragraphs: Murle elders remain important sources of linguistic and historical knowledge. Many elders know words, expressions, stories and place names that younger generations may hear less frequently.
Their knowledge can include traditional vocabulary that is not always found in modern written materials. Recording elders' speech can therefore preserve information that might otherwise disappear.
Young people can play an equally important role by learning from elders, documenting their knowledge and using Murle in modern forms of communication.

Language preservation is strongest when knowledge moves in both directions: elders pass traditional knowledge to younger generations, while younger people use modern tools to preserve and share that knowledge.

body.heading: Preserving Murle for Future Generations
paragraphs: Preserving Murle requires more than creating a dictionary. A living language survives when people continue to use it in families, communities, education, storytelling, cultural activities and everyday communication.

Useful preservation efforts can include recording elders, collecting traditional stories, documenting proverbs, creating children's reading materials, developing dictionaries, preserving place names and producing educational resources in Murle.

Digital platforms can make this work more accessible. Audio recordings can preserve pronunciation, while written archives can preserve vocabulary and stories. Mobile applications can bring language resources directly to young people.

The goal should not be to freeze Murle in an imagined past. The goal is to ensure that Murle remains a living language capable of expressing both traditional knowledge and the experiences of future generations.

body.heading: The Language as a Historical Record
paragraphs: Every generation leaves traces in its language. New words appear, older expressions become less common and meanings can change. These changes can provide clues about social and historical developments.

Murle vocabulary contains knowledge connected to the environment, livestock, social relationships and cultural institutions. Studying this vocabulary can therefore contribute to a broader understanding of Murle history.

At the same time, linguistic evidence must be interpreted carefully. A single word cannot prove a migration or historical event by itself. Historical conclusions require comparison across many forms of evidence.
The Murle language should therefore be treated both as a living means of communication and as an important source of evidence about the long history of its speakers.

body.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The Murle language is one of the most important inheritances carried through the history of the Murle people. It connects generations, preserves cultural knowledge and provides a means through which communities understand and describe their world.

Its relationship to the Surmic language family provides evidence of historical connections between Murle and other peoples of the wider eastern African region. At the same time, Murle has developed as a distinct language belonging to a distinct people.
From Boma to Pibor and beyond, Murle speakers have maintained their language while adapting to changing environments and changing political and social circumstances.

The future of the language depends on its continued use. Elders preserve knowledge from earlier generations, while young Murle have the opportunity to carry that knowledge into schools, books, phones, applications, recordings and other forms of modern communication.

To preserve Murle language is therefore to preserve history. Every word remembered, every story recorded, every proverb taught and every child who learns to speak Murle becomes part of the continuing journey of the people.

historicalNote: Murle is classified within the Surmic group of languages. Linguistic relationships can provide evidence about historical connections between populations, but language classification should not be treated as a complete migration history. Regional differences in speech and vocabulary may exist among Murle communities. This article emphasizes the importance of Murle oral knowledge and community participation in documenting and preserving the language.
